docs.title: Exploratory Data Analysis — 2026.2
docs.text: Project for Insper's Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning, semester 2026.2: an exploratory data analysis (EDA) and preprocessing pipeline that prepares tabular data for a neural network. We did it for both tasks: a classification dataset and a regression dataset. No model is trained here; each report ends with a synthesis for whoever builds the model.

docs.title: The two analyses
docs.text:
• Classification — UCI Bank Marketing

    Will a client subscribe to a term deposit after a marketing call?

    • 45,211 calls, 16 input features, binary target y
    • Imbalanced: 11.70% yes
    • duration dropped as target leakage
    • Stratified 80/20 split; 51 features after the pipeline

    Start reading · Full report on one page

  • Regression — UCI Seoul Bike Sharing Demand

    How many public bikes are rented in Seoul in a given hour?

    • 8,760 hours, 13 input columns, target rented_bike_count
    • Right-skewed target: train on sqrt(y)
    • Closed hours removed as target leakage
    • Split by whole days, stratified by season; 22 features after the pipeline

    Start reading · Full report on one page

Both reports follow the same stages from the assignment. Each stage is its own page (use the tabs at the top and Next at the bottom of each page), and each report is also available on a single page:

Stage Content 0. Proposal dataset, target, motivation, first risk 1. Initial inspection data dictionary, quality and leakage, target, train/test split 2. Univariate analysis numerical and categorical distributions 3. Bivariate and multivariate analysis correlations, feature vs target, grouped boxplots 4. Preprocessing strategies, PCA / t-SNE / UMAP, Pipeline + ColumnTransformer 5. Synthesis main findings, risks and plan, 10-item summary table

docs.title: 0. Proposal
docs.text:
Classification EDA, section 1 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

Structure: stages 0-3 (Part 1) and stages 4-5 (Part 2). No model is trained anywhere in this report.

Item Value Dataset UCI Bank Marketing, older full version: bank-full.csv URL https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank%2Bmarketing Size (original) 45,211 rows x 17 columns (16 input features + target) Target y: did the client subscribe to a term deposit? (yes / no, binary) Features (original) 7 numerical, 9 categorical (verified from the data, see 1A) Features (after excluding duration) 6 numerical, 9 categorical = 15 predictors Approval status Approved by the instructor.

Motivation. Direct-marketing calls are expensive, and only 11.70% of the contacted clients in this dataset subscribed. A classifier that ranks clients by their chance of subscribing before a call is made could help the bank prioritise calls. The dataset is real (a Portuguese bank, May 2008 to November 2010), well documented, and has a mix of numerical and categorical features and a clear binary target, so it fits a classification EDA.

First risk. The target is imbalanced (11.70% yes, ratio 7.55 : 1), and the strongest single input, duration, is target leakage: it is only known after the call. We exclude it (see 1B), so realistic predictive signal will be weaker than published benchmarks that use it. A second risk is that the file is chronological and the subscription rate drifts strongly over time (1B).

Download steps (reproduced by scripts/part1_download_data.py):

  1. Download https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/222/bank+marketing.zip (the download link on the UCI page above).
  2. The archive contains two nested zips: bank.zip (older version) and bank-additional.zip (newer version). Only bank.zip is used.
  3. Extract bank-full.csv and bank-names.txt from bank.zip to data/raw/. The file is ;-separated with quoted strings and a header row.
  4. bank-additional-names.txt is also extracted, only as documentation: it holds UCI's official note on duration leakage (quoted in 1B). No bank-additional data is used.
  5. Recorded: download time 2026-10-13T21:56:18+00:00 (UTC); bank-full.csv is 4,610,348 bytes, SHA-256 d1513ec63b385506f7cfce9f2c5caa9fe99e7ba4e8c3fa264b3aaf0f849ed32d (see data/raw/part1_download_log.json).

What a row is. One row is one client contacted in a direct-marketing phone campaign, with the attributes of their last contact in the current campaign. The file has 45,211 rows ordered by date (May 2008 to November 2010). UCI notes that a client often needed more than one contact; campaign counts them.

Schema check. Read with pandas.read_csv(sep=";"): 45,211 rows x 17 columns. Columns with an integer dtype (int64) are the numerical features (7). Columns with an object dtype other than y are the categorical features (9). This matches the expected 7 + 9 + target. The script asserts this, so it fails if the file changes.

docs.title: 1B. Data quality
docs.text:
Missing values. There are 0 NaN values in the whole file. Missing information is instead coded as the literal level "unknown" in job, education, contact, poutcome.

column NaN count NaN % "unknown" count "unknown" % age 0 0.00 0 0.00 job 0 0.00 288 0.64 marital 0 0.00 0 0.00 education 0 0.00 1857 4.11 default 0 0.00 0 0.00 balance 0 0.00 0 0.00 housing 0 0.00 0 0.00 loan 0 0.00 0 0.00 contact 0 0.00 13020 28.80 day 0 0.00 0 0.00 month 0 0.00 0 0.00 duration 0 0.00 0 0.00 campaign 0 0.00 0 0.00 pdays 0 0.00 0 0.00 previous 0 0.00 0 0.00 poutcome 0 0.00 36959 81.75 y 0 0.00 0 0.00
  • "unknown" counts on the full data: job 288 (0.64%), education 1,857 (4.11%), contact 13,020 (28.80%), poutcome 36,959 (81.75%). 37,369 rows (82.65%) have at least one "unknown". Excluding poutcome, the figure is 14,304 rows (31.64%). Dropping such rows is therefore not an option.
  • Decision: keep "unknown" as its own category. The data supports this. (i) For poutcome, "unknown" is structural: it almost exactly marks "not previously contacted" (see the pdays section). (ii) For contact, "unknown" is a recording-practice artifact: the first 12,657 rows in file (time) order are all "unknown", and 97.21% of all contact = "unknown" rows fall in the first 30% of the file. (iii) "unknown" levels have their own subscription rates (for contact: 4.07% vs 14.78% when known). This means the values are not missing completely at random, and imputing them with the mode would erase signal.

Duplicates. There are 0 exact duplicate rows among all 17 columns. After duration is excluded, 16 rows duplicate an earlier row (31 rows involved, in 15 groups). None of these groups has conflicting labels (0 groups with different y). Decision: keep them. They differed only by call duration, so they are most likely different contacts with identical profiles rather than copy errors, and they are a negligible share of the data.

pdays = -1 sentinel. UCI documents -1 as "client was not previously contacted". It is not an impossible value but a code, and the data confirms this:

  • 36,954 rows (81.74%) have pdays = -1. Exactly the same rows have previous = 0 (36,954 rows; 0 mismatches).
  • No other negative value and no pdays = 0 exist (0 and 0 rows). Real values run from 1 to 871 days.
  • Treating -1 as a number is misleading. The mean of pdays is 40.20 with the sentinel and 224.58 among previously contacted clients only.
  • Cross-tab with poutcome:
pdays group failure other success unknown pdays = -1 0 0 0 36954 pdays >= 1 4901 1840 1511 5
  • Subscription rate: 9.16% for never-contacted clients vs 23.07% for previously contacted ones. The sentinel is informative, so the "not previously contacted" information must be preserved in preprocessing (for example, a binary flag plus a pdays value that is masked or neutral for those clients).

Impossible, inconsistent and implausible values (full data):

check rows interpretation action age < 18 or > 100 0 impossible for a bank client contact list none age > 90 7 plausible but extreme keep day outside 1-31 0 impossible none day exceeds days in its month (e.g. 31 apr, 30 feb) 0 impossible calendar date none campaign < 1 (must include the last contact) 0 impossible by definition none previous < 0 0 impossible none pdays < -1, or pdays = 0 0 impossible / undefined code none pdays = -1 while previous > 0 (or the reverse) 0 inconsistent none poutcome = unknown while previous > 0 5 inconsistent: a previous contact exists but its outcome is unrecorded keep; treat as category poutcome known while previous = 0 0 inconsistent none balance < 0 3766 valid: overdrawn account (balance is not bounded at 0) keep duration = 0 s 3 consistent with no conversation; all have y = no moot: duration excluded job = student and age > 40 10 implausible but possible keep job = retired and age < 40 25 implausible but possible (early/disability retirement) keep
  • No impossible values were found. The only true inconsistency is 5 rows with previous > 0 but poutcome = "unknown". These are kept, because the category already represents "unrecorded".
  • balance < 0 in 3,766 rows (8.33%) is not an error: the average balance of an overdrawn account can be negative.

Outliers. These are quantified with the 1.5 x IQR rule on the training set in 2A (Figure 3). Decision: no outliers are removed in Part 1. Extreme balance, campaign and previous values are plausible, and removing them would change the population. Part 2 should prefer robust or monotone transforms (see Handoff).

Identifiers and constants. There is no ID column. The highest unique-value ratio is balance with 7,168 distinct values (0.159 of rows), which is a measurement, not an identifier. There are 0 constant columns. The most dominant level is in default (98.20% no; default = yes has only 815 rows, 1.80%). It is nearly constant but kept, as Part 2 can decide whether it carries enough signal.

Leakage investigation.

  1. duration (excluded). UCI's attribute note (in bank-additional-names.txt from the same official archive) says: "this attribute highly affects the output target (e.g., if duration=0 then y='no'). Yet, the duration is not known before a call is performed. Also, after the end of the call y is obviously known. Thus, this input should only be included for benchmark purposes and should be discarded if the intention is to have a realistic predictive model." The data confirms this:
  2. Spearman correlation of duration with y is 0.342. The highest correlation among the other numerical features is 0.169 (previous).
  3. There are 3 rows with duration = 0. All of them have y = no (check result: yes), exactly as UCI's note says.
  4. The subscription rate rises steadily with call length:
duration (s) rows subscribed subscription rate % 0 3 0 0.00 1-60 4763 9 0.19 61-120 9278 202 2.18 121-300 18893 1620 8.57 301-600 8484 1625 19.15 601-4918 3790 1833 48.36

Our task is to predict subscription before calling, so duration cannot be a predictor. It is dropped before the split and is not analysed further.

  1. Row order (time) - not a column, but a leakage risk. The file is sorted by date. Splitting the rows into deciles by file position shows strong drift: the subscription rate goes from 3.0% in the first decile to 47.1% in the last.
row decile (file order) rows subscription rate % contact = unknown % poutcome = unknown % D1 4522 3.0 100.0 100.0 D2 4521 3.7 100.0 100.0 D3 4521 4.8 79.9 100.0 D4 4521 6.4 0.5 100.0 D5 4521 6.1 0.2 100.0 D6 4521 6.2 1.6 83.0 D7 4520 10.5 0.1 71.4 D8 4522 13.1 0.0 61.1 D9 4521 16.1 0.0 60.7 D10 4521 47.1 5.6 41.2

The row index must never be used as a feature. A random stratified split (required here) mixes periods, so test performance will be optimistic about the future. We record this as a limitation; it is not corrected in Part 1.

  1. poutcome, pdays and previous describe previous campaigns, so they are known before the call. campaign includes the current (last) call, but the number of attempts so far is known when deciding on the next call, so it is kept. contact, day and month describe the last contact. They are plausible as scheduling attributes, but their link to the data-collection period (see contact above) should be kept in mind.

Columns dropped and reasons.

Column Reason duration Target leakage: only known during or after the call (UCI note and evidence above).

No other columns are dropped. Result: original 45,211 x 17 (7 numerical + 9 categorical + y); after the exclusion 45,211 x 16 (6 numerical + 9 categorical + y). No rows are removed.

Figure 1 - conclusion. - age is unimodal and mildly right-skewed (skew 0.69). The mean (40.89) is above the median (39.00), and the mode is 32. 95.50% of clients are 25-60. A thin tail above about 60 holds the IQR outliers (394, 1.09%), which are real older clients. - balance is extremely right-skewed (skew 8.34). The mean of 1,365.49 is three times the median of 451.00, and there is a spike at exactly 0 (7.77% of clients). 8.30% are negative (min -8,019) and the max is 102,127. The plot is clipped to P1-P99 [-626, 13,161] for readability. - day has no skew (0.09) and no outliers, but it is multimodal, with peaks on specific days (20 (6.1%), 18 (5.0%), 21 (4.5%)) and uneven counts across the month. This reflects call scheduling rather than a smooth quantity.

Figure 2 - conclusion. - campaign is a heavy-tailed count (skew 4.94). The mode is 1 contact (38.78% of clients), 78.69% received at most 3, and 945 clients received more than 10 (max 63). - pdays applies only to previously contacted clients (18.20%). Its distribution is multimodal (median 195.00, IQR 133.00-328.00). The most frequent values are 182 (128), 92 (114), 91 (100), 183 (95), 181 (92) days, i.e. clients re-contacted about three or six months after the previous campaign. Figure 2 also shows a further cluster just under 400 days. - previous among contacted clients has a median of 2.00 and a mode of 1, with a very long tail up to 275 (skew 28.55).

Figure 3 - conclusion. Using the 1.5 x IQR rule: - balance has the most real outliers (3,770, 10.42%), on both sides. campaign has 2,465 (6.82%) and age 394 (1.09%). - For pdays and previous, the IQR collapses to the single sentinel value (Q1 = Q3 = -1.00 and 0.00). Every previously contacted client (6,584) is therefore flagged as an "outlier". This is an artifact of the sentinel, not evidence of bad data. Within contacted clients, there are only 40 outliers for pdays and 367 for previous. - 4 features have |skew| > 1 (balance, campaign, pdays, previous). This motivates rank-based correlation in 3A, and transforms (log/Yeo-Johnson, or binning) and/or robust scaling in Part 2.

docs.title: 3A. Numerical x numerical
docs.text:
Choice: Spearman. 4 of the 6 numerical features are strongly skewed (balance, campaign, pdays, previous), and pdays/previous are dominated by a sentinel/zero mass. Pearson assumes linear relationships and is sensitive to extreme values, while Spearman uses ranks: it captures monotone relationships and is robust to outliers. Pearson is shown only for comparison.

Top pairs by |Spearman|:

pair spearman pearson pdays - previous 0.986 0.439 day - campaign 0.139 0.162 campaign - pdays -0.112 -0.089 campaign - previous -0.108 -0.031 age - balance 0.096 0.096 day - pdays -0.093 -0.093

Figure 6 - conclusion. - The only strongly correlated pair is pdays - previous: Spearman 0.986, compared with Pearson 0.439. Pearson understates it because the relationship is monotone but far from linear (a large sentinel mass plus long tails). - All other pairs have |rho| <= 0.139. The next strongest are day - campaign (0.139) and campaign - pdays (-0.112). Apart from the pair above, the numerical features are close to non-redundant.

Figure 7 - conclusion. The 0.986 correlation is driven almost entirely by the shared sentinel, since pdays = -1 exactly when previous = 0 (1B). Among previously contacted clients, Spearman is only -0.099 (Pearson -0.016), so the actual magnitudes are nearly unrelated. Redundancy: the two features duplicate the binary "previously contacted" information, not their values. Part 2 should encode that flag once and keep both magnitudes (or test dropping one) instead of treating them as collinear duplicates.

docs.title: 3B. Categorical x target
docs.text:
The training base rate is 11.70%. Rates for every level of every categorical feature, with 95% Wilson intervals and lift, are in part1_outputs/categorical_target_rates_train.csv. The spread between each feature's highest and lowest level rate:

feature max - min rate (pp) poutcome 55.4 month 44.2 job 21.6 contact 10.7 housing 9.0 education 6.3 default 5.9 loan 5.8 marital 5.0

The features with the largest spread are poutcome (55.4 pp), month (44.2 pp), job (21.6 pp). The smallest is marital (5.0 pp). The selected figures cover the strongest and most decision-relevant features.

Figure 8 - conclusion. - poutcome separates the classes most. Clients whose previous campaign was a success subscribe at 64.6%, against 12.3% (failure), 16.5% (other) and 9.2% (unknown = never contacted). - contact = unknown has a much lower rate (4.1%) than cellular (14.8%) and telephone (13.9%). This matches the early-period artifact found in 1B, so it partly encodes time. - Clients without a housing loan (16.7% vs 7.7%) or without a personal loan (12.6% vs 6.8%) subscribe more often. - The intervals for poutcome = success, contact = unknown, housing and loan do not overlap with their contrasts. cellular and telephone overlap, so the contact channel itself adds little once unknown is separated out.

Figure 9 - conclusion. Contact volume and subscription rate move in opposite directions (Spearman correlation across the 12 months: -0.87). - The busiest month has the lowest rate: may (6.7%, n = 11,062). - Low-volume months have rates above 30%: mar (50.9%, n = 391), sep (45.2%, n = 451), oct (43.8%, n = 592), dec (47.2%, n = 178). The maximum is mar (50.9%, n = 391). - Volume and rate are drawn as two panels on separate axes, not as a dual-axis chart. - month is strongly predictive, but given the drift found in 1B it likely mixes seasonality with the period of data collection (there is no year column). Its confidence intervals are wide for the thin months.

Figure 10 - conclusion. - job: students (28.9%) and retired clients (23.0%) subscribe far above the base rate. Blue-collar clients (7.3%), housemaids (8.4%), entrepreneurs (8.5%) and services workers (8.9%) subscribe below it. - education: the rate increases from primary (8.6%) to secondary (10.7%) to tertiary (14.9%). unknown (13.2%) has a wide interval, consistent with its small size. - These features carry moderate, roughly ordinal signal. job = unknown (12.0%) has a very wide interval and is too small to interpret.

docs.title: 3C. Numerical x categorical (grouped boxplots, split by y)

docs.title: 4. Preprocessing
docs.text:
Classification EDA, section 5 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

Everything in this stage is implemented in code/bank_preprocessing.py (a scikit-learn Pipeline + ColumnTransformer) and run by scripts/part2_eda.py. The intended model is a neural network, which needs a dense, fully numerical input on comparable scales.

Consistency with Part 1. Before anything is fitted, the script recomputes 25 quantities from the raw file and stops if any differs from the values saved by Part 1 (part1_outputs/). All agree; the full list is in the Appendix. In particular, the split is the one from 1D, row for row: train 36,168 rows, test 9,043 rows.

No fitting on test data. Clip bounds, the Yeo-Johnson parameter, means, standard deviations and one-hot levels are learned by fit(X_train). The test set only goes through transform. PCA, t-SNE and UMAP (4B) use training rows only.

docs.title: 4A. Strategies
docs.text: Each choice below starts from a check on the data and from a finding of Part 1.

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text:
Check. There are 0 NaN values in the training predictors and 0 in the test predictors (Part 1, 1B: 0 in the whole file). So there is nothing to impute in this dataset.

Table 4.1 - Categorical checks before encoding (training set; last column compares with the test set).

feature NaN (train) "unknown" rows (train) "unknown" % (train) levels (train) test levels unseen in train job 0 234 0.65 12 0 marital 0 0 0.00 3 0 education 0 1482 4.10 4 0 default 0 0 0.00 2 0 housing 0 0 0.00 2 0 loan 0 0 0.00 2 0 contact 0 10386 28.72 3 0 month 0 0 0.00 12 0 poutcome 0 29589 81.81 4 0

Strategy.

  • "unknown" stays a category. Part 1 (1B) showed that it is not missing at random: for poutcome it marks clients who were never contacted, for contact it marks the early period of the file, and its subscription rate differs (4.1% for contact = unknown against 14.8% for cellular, Figure 8). Replacing it with the mode would erase that signal, so it is one-hot encoded like any other level.
  • pdays = -1 is treated as "not applicable", not as a number. Part 1 (1B, Figure 7) showed that -1 is a code for "not previously contacted" and coincides exactly with previous = 0. The pipeline replaces -1 by a missing value, standardises pdays with the mean and standard deviation of previously contacted training clients only (225.09 and 115.32 days, n = 6,584), then fills the masked rows with 0 and adds the indicator column missingindicator_pdays. The value 0 is the contacted-client mean, so it is neutral, and the indicator carries the "not previously contacted" information that Part 1 asked to preserve. In the training set the indicator is 1 for 29,584 rows (81.80%).
  • Imputers are safeguards. The pipeline still contains a median imputer for the numerical features and a constant "unknown" imputer for the categorical ones, fitted on the training set. They change 0 values here. They exist so that transform does not fail if future data contains a NaN. A NaN in a categorical feature would join the existing "unknown" level, which is consistent with the decision above.

docs.title: Outliers
docs.text:
Check. Part 1 (2A, Figure 3) counted 1.5 x IQR outliers in the training set: balance 3,770 (10.42%), campaign 2,465, and for pdays/previous an artifact of the sentinel. No value was impossible (1B), so Part 1 removed no rows and recommended caps or transforms fitted on train. Expressed as z-scores of the raw training values, the extremes reach 32.8 (balance), 19.4 (campaign) and 113.9 (previous) standard deviations. Inputs of that size would dominate the gradients of a neural network.

Strategy: clip (winsorise), then transform. No row is removed.

  • balance, campaign and previous are clipped to the 1st and 99th percentiles of the training set. For the two counts the 1st percentile equals the minimum, so only the upper tail is clipped.
  • balance then goes through a Yeo-Johnson power transform (fitted lambda 0.818). It is used instead of a logarithm because -626.33 is negative: overdrawn accounts are valid (1B).
  • campaign and previous are counts, so they get log1p. This matches Part 1's finding that the signal of campaign is in the tail and has diminishing returns (Figure 13).
  • Why clipping is needed, not only a transform. Yeo-Johnson on the unclipped balance still leaves standardised values between -33.8 and 21.1. After clipping the range is -3.32 to 4.16.
  • age and day are not clipped. age is only mildly skewed (0.69) and its extremes are informative: clients aged 60+ subscribe at 33.7% against 9.8% for ages 30-59 (Figure 11). day has no outliers (Figure 3).
  • pdays is not clipped. Once the sentinel is masked, it has few outliers among contacted clients (2A) and its standardised range is -1.94 to 5.60.

Table 4.2 - Rows changed by clipping. Bounds are learned on the training set and applied unchanged to the test set.

feature lower bound (train P1) upper bound (train P99) train rows below train rows above train rows clipped train % test rows clipped test % balance -626.33 13,161.32 362 362 724 2.00 184 2.03 campaign 1.00 16.33 0 362 362 1.00 89 0.98 previous 0.00 9.00 0 296 296 0.82 65 0.72 any of the three - - - - 1,372 3.79 333 3.68

1,372 training rows (3.79%) have at least one clipped value, and 333 test rows (3.68%). Clipped training rows subscribe at 10.1%, against 11.8% for the others. Clipping keeps their rank at the top of the scale but removes the distinction among them, which is the cost of this strategy.

docs.title: Categorical encoding
docs.text:
• One-hot encoding with OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), with no reference level dropped. Part 1 (2B, Figure 5) found low cardinality: at most 12 levels per feature and 44 levels in total. The features are nominal (month is cyclical and education has an unknown level), so integer codes would impose an order that the data does not have.
  • Unseen categories. The test set contains 0 levels that are absent from the training set (Table 4.1). handle_unknown="ignore" is still set: a level that appears later is encoded as all zeros for that feature instead of raising an error. This matters most for the rare levels found in Part 1 (job: unknown; month: dec).
  • No level is dropped because a neural network does not need a reference category, and dropping one would make the all-zeros row of an unseen level indistinguishable from the reference level.
  • Rare levels are not grouped. Part 1 suggested grouping only if a model overfits, which cannot be judged before modelling.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Choice: standardisation (zero mean, unit variance), fitted on the training set, applied after clipping and transforming.

  • A neural network is trained by gradient descent on weighted sums of its inputs. Features on very different scales (balance in thousands of euros, campaign in single units) give badly conditioned gradients and make one learning rate unsuitable for all weights. Standard weight initialisation also assumes inputs centred near zero with variance near one.
  • Min-max scaling was not chosen because the maximum would be set by the tail: the bulk of balance would be squeezed into a small part of [0, 1].
  • Robust scaling alone was not chosen because it centres and scales by median and IQR but leaves the extremes large. Clipping bounds the tails, and after that the mean and standard deviation are no longer dominated by a few points (the concern raised in 2A).
  • One-hot columns and the indicator stay as 0/1. They are already bounded and on a scale comparable to standardised features.

docs.title: 4B. Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
Input. The 51 preprocessed features of the training set only (4C). Points are coloured by the target.

Sample. PCA is fitted on all 36,168 training rows. t-SNE and UMAP are computed on a sample, because t-SNE is slow on the full set and a scatter of 36 thousand points is unreadable. The sample is 5,000 training rows (13.8% of train), drawn with train_test_split(train_size=5000, stratify=y_train, random_state=42). It keeps the class balance: 585 yes (11.70%). The same sample is used in Figures 17 to 20, and all methods use random_state=42.

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
Table 4.4 - Explained variance of the first 10 principal components.

component explained variance % cumulative % PC1 14.90 14.90 PC2 12.55 27.45 PC3 11.22 38.68 PC4 9.76 48.43 PC5 8.61 57.04 PC6 6.65 63.69 PC7 4.46 68.15 PC8 3.78 71.93 PC9 3.21 75.14 PC10 2.71 77.85

Figure 15 - conclusion. - PC1 + PC2 explain 27.45% of the variance (PC1 14.90%, PC2 12.55%). A 2D PCA plot therefore hides almost three quarters of the variance. - Variance is spread over many directions: 11 components are needed for 80%, 18 for 90% and 24 for 95%. There is no low-dimensional linear structure, which agrees with the near-zero correlations among numerical features found in 3A (Figure 6). - The last 9 components have zero variance. This is expected: each of the 9 one-hot groups sums to 1, which gives 9 exact linear dependencies. - The 6 numerical columns carry 52.9% of the total variance and the 45 binary columns 47.1%, because a 0/1 column has variance of at most 0.25. PCA therefore weights numerical features more than categorical ones. This is a property of the encoding and not evidence that the numerical features are more important for y.

Table 4.5 - Largest loadings of PC1 and PC2.

PC1 feature PC1 loading PC2 feature PC2 loading previous +0.732 age +0.739 campaign -0.348 balance +0.495 day -0.307 campaign +0.186 missingindicator_pdays -0.277 housing_no +0.168 poutcome_unknown -0.276 housing_yes -0.168 poutcome_failure +0.164 marital_single -0.166 balance +0.156 marital_married +0.143 contact_cellular +0.113 month_may -0.125

Figure 16 - conclusion (loadings). - PC1 is a "contact history" axis. It has previous (+0.73) at one end and the not-previously-contacted indicator (-0.28) and poutcome_unknown (-0.28) at the other. These three move together, as Part 1 found (1B; Figure 7). campaign (-0.35) and day (-0.31) have the opposite sign to previous, consistent with their small negative correlations with previous and pdays in 3A. The magnitude of pdays has almost no weight (-0.01), which matches the finding that pdays and previous are nearly unrelated once the sentinel is removed (Spearman -0.099). - PC2 is an "age and wealth" axis. It is led by age (+0.74) and balance (+0.50), with housing_no, marital_married on the same side and housing_yes, marital_single on the other: older clients with higher balances and no housing loan. - The five largest loadings account for 90.4% of PC1 and 88.2% of PC2 (sum of squared loadings), so each axis is described by a handful of features. month and job, which had large subscription-rate spreads in 3B, barely appear, for the variance reason given above.

Figure 17 - conclusion. - The projection shows two clouds along PC1. From the loadings, the right-hand cloud is the previously contacted clients and the large left-hand cloud is the never-contacted majority. - The classes overlap in both clouds. yes points are relatively more frequent on the right, but no line separates them. The class means differ by +0.59 pooled standard deviations on PC1 and by +0.22 on PC2 (all training rows). - A linear view of the two highest-variance directions is therefore not enough to separate subscribers. This is expected, since PCA does not use y and these two components hold only 27.45% of the variance.

docs.title: t-SNE
docs.text:
Perplexities compared: 5, 30, 50. Settings: init="pca", learning_rate="auto", default number of iterations, random_state=42.

Figure 18 - conclusion. - Perplexity 5 breaks the data into many tiny groups of near-identical profiles. Only very local neighbourhoods are kept and no larger structure is visible. - Perplexity 30 and 50 show one island that is separated from the main mass and has a visibly higher density of yes points. The main mass contains smaller pockets where yes is more frequent, but most of it is mixed. - The island appears at both larger perplexities, so it is not an artifact of a single setting. The layout of the main mass changes between panels and should not be interpreted.

docs.title: UMAP
docs.text:
n_neighbors compared: 5, 15, 50. Settings: min_dist=0.1, Euclidean metric, random_state=42.

Figure 19 - conclusion. - All three settings isolate one compact island with a high share of yes, the same structure that t-SNE finds. - With n_neighbors = 5 and 15, the remaining points form two further groups. With n_neighbors = 50, which gives more weight to global structure, these two groups join into one connected mass while the first island stays apart. - Inside the two large groups, yes and no are mixed, with yes slightly concentrated along some edges.

Figure 20 - conclusion. Colouring the same embeddings by two features identified in Part 1 explains the islands: - The isolated island is the previously contacted clients (n = 858 in the sample, subscription rate 23.3%). - The other two groups are never-contacted clients, split by whether contact is unknown (n = 1,422, rate 4.4%) or known (n = 2,720, rate 11.9%). - The visible structure is therefore defined by contact history and by the recording period (1B showed that contact = unknown marks the early part of the file), not by the target. The groups differ in subscription rate, but within each group the classes are mixed.

docs.title: What t-SNE and UMAP reveal relative to PCA
docs.text:
• PCA gives one interpretable linear axis (contact history) and shows two overlapping clouds. It hides the contact = unknown group, because that group differs in binary columns with little variance.
  • t-SNE and UMAP use local neighbourhoods in all 51 dimensions. They separate the previously contacted clients cleanly, and UMAP also separates the contact = unknown group. These groups are defined by categorical features that PCA down-weights.
  • None of the three methods separates yes from no. All three agree that subscribers are more frequent among previously contacted clients and are otherwise spread through the majority. The class boundary is not a simple low-dimensional one, so a model will need non-linear combinations of features, and high accuracy on the minority class should not be expected from these inputs alone.

Interpretation limits. In t-SNE and UMAP plots, the size of a cluster, the distance between clusters and the density of points have no direct quantitative interpretation. The axes have arbitrary units. Both methods preserve neighbourhoods, not distances: a large island is not a large or spread-out group, and two islands that are far apart are not "more different" than two that are close. The layouts also change with perplexity, n_neighbors and the random seed. Only structure that persists across settings (here, the previously contacted island) is treated as a finding, and it was confirmed with the original features (Figure 20), not from the plot alone. These embeddings are diagnostic plots only; they are not used as model inputs.

docs.text:
build_preprocessor() in code/bank_preprocessing.py returns an unfitted Pipeline whose single step is this ColumnTransformer:

docs.title: 5. Synthesis
docs.text: Classification EDA, section 6 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

docs.title: 5A. Main findings
docs.text: # Finding Evidence 1 The data is clean in the usual sense: 0 NaN, 0 exact duplicate rows, no impossible values. Missing information is coded as "unknown", mostly in poutcome (full data: 36,959 (81.75%)) and contact (13,020 (28.80%)). 1B missing-value and consistency tables; Figure 5; Table 4.1 2 The target is imbalanced: 11.70% yes, ratio 7.55 : 1. Always predicting no gives 88.30% accuracy. 1C table; 1D table 3 duration is target leakage and is excluded. It is the only dropped column. 1B leakage table (duration bins) 4 The file is chronological and the subscription rate drifts from 3.0% to 47.1% across row deciles. contact = unknown and month partly encode the period. 1B row-decile table; Figures 8 and 9 5 pdays = -1 is a code for "not previously contacted" (81.74% of rows) and coincides with previous = 0. The 0.986 Spearman correlation of pdays - previous comes from this shared code; among contacted clients it is -0.099. 1B sentinel table; Figures 6 and 7 6 Contact history is the strongest signal: poutcome = success subscribes at 64.6% against 9.2% for never-contacted clients. It is also the main axis of variance (PC1) and the group that t-SNE and UMAP isolate. Figure 8; Figures 16, 18, 19, 20 7 month has a large rate spread, from may (6.7%, n = 11,062) to mar (50.9%, n = 391), with volume and rate moving in opposite directions. Figure 9; 3B spread table 8 Numerical effects are non-linear: the age effect is U-shaped (33.7% for 60+ against 9.8% for 30-59) and repeated calls have diminishing returns (14.6% after one contact, 5.9% after more than five). Figures 11 and 13 9 balance, campaign and previous are heavy-tailed (skew 8.34, 4.94, 45.03). Clipping at train P1-P99 changes 1,372 training rows (3.79%) and, with a transform and standardisation, bounds every input to within 5.60 standard deviations. Figures 1-3; Tables 4.2 and 4.3; Figure 14 10 There is no low-dimensional linear structure and no clean class separation: PC1 + PC2 explain 27.45%, 18 components are needed for 90%, and the classes overlap in PCA, t-SNE and UMAP. Table 4.4; Figures 15, 17, 18, 19 11 The preprocessing pipeline turns 15 predictors into 51 features with no NaN: train 36,168 x 51, test 9,043 x 51. 4C verification table; Table 4.6

docs.title: 5B. Modelling risks and handling plan
docs.text: # Risk Evidence Handling plan 1 Class imbalance (7.55 : 1). Accuracy is misleading and a network can collapse to predicting no. 1C Keep stratification in every split and in cross-validation. Report PR-AUC, recall and precision on yes and balanced accuracy, with the 88.30% majority baseline for reference. Use class weights in the loss, computed on the training set. Choose the decision threshold on a validation set, never on the test set. 2 Time drift and an optimistic split. The random stratified split mixes periods, so test performance overstates performance on future campaigns. 1B row-decile table State this limitation with every result. As a sensitivity check, also evaluate with a chronological split (train on the first 80% of rows, test on the last 20%) and report the gap. Never use the row index as a feature. 3 Period proxies. contact = unknown and month may be learned as "which period" instead of a client property. 1B; Figures 8, 9 and 20 Train an ablation without contact and month and compare. If the chronological check (risk 2) shows a large drop, prefer the model without them. 4 Leakage. duration would inflate every metric. 1B duration is never loaded by load_data(). Keep all fitted preprocessing inside the pipeline so that cross-validation refits it on each training fold. 5 Redundant "never contacted" information. The indicator, poutcome_unknown and previous = 0 say almost the same thing (they differ in 5 training rows). 1B; 3A; Figure 16 Harmless for prediction with a neural network, but it makes single weights uninterpretable. Use weight decay, and do not read importance from individual weights. Test dropping the indicator. 6 Rare levels and near-constant columns (job: unknown; month: dec; default = yes is 1.80%). Their weights are estimated from few rows and can overfit. 2B; Figures 5 and 9 Weight decay or dropout plus early stopping on a validation set. If validation shows overfitting, group the rare months and test dropping default. handle_unknown="ignore" covers levels missing from a fold. 7 Clipping removes information about the 3.79% most extreme clients. Table 4.2 The clip quantiles are parameters of QuantileClipper. Treat them as a hyperparameter (for example P0.5-P99.5, or no clipping) and select on validation data only. 8 Weak, non-linear signal. No projection separates the classes, and the age and campaign effects are non-linear. Figures 11, 13, 17, 18, 19 Start from a logistic-regression baseline on the same features, then a small network with hidden layers. Expect modest gains, and compare against the baseline instead of against published results that use duration. 9 Over-reading the embeddings. t-SNE and UMAP cluster sizes and distances are not quantitative. 4B Use them only as diagnostics. docs.title: 0. Proposal
docs.text:
Regression EDA, section 1 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

All statistics after 1D are computed on the training set only. No model is trained anywhere in this report.

Item Value Dataset UCI Seoul Bike Sharing Demand: SeoulBikeData.csv URL https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/560/seoul+bike+sharing+demand Size (original) 8,760 rows x 14 columns (13 input columns + target) Target rented_bike_count: number of public bikes rented in Seoul in that hour (count, continuous for regression) Features (original) 9 numerical, 3 categorical, 1 date Approval status Approved by the instructor.

Motivation. Seoul's public bike system must have bikes available at the right hour. Predicting hourly demand from the time of day, the calendar and the weather is a regression problem that has a direct operational use (rebalancing, staffing). The data are real, cover a full year (2017-12-01 to 2018-11-30) and mix numerical weather readings with categorical calendar features.

First risk. Consecutive hours are strongly dependent. A row-level random split would put 10 h of a day in train and 11 h of the same day in test, which inflates test scores. We split by whole days (1D).

docs.title: 1B. Data quality
docs.text:
Missing values. 0 NaN in all 14 columns (0.00% everywhere). The file does have disguised missing values: humidity == 0 in 17 hours (0.19%), all on five days in May 2018 (2018-05-19, 05-21, 05-22, 05-27, 05-28). 0% relative humidity is physically impossible in Seoul, so these are sensor faults. They are treated as missing in 4A.

Duplicates. 0 duplicated rows and 0 duplicated (date, hour) pairs.

Consistency checks (outputs/consistency_checks.csv):

Check Rows hour outside 0-23 0 humidity outside 0-100 0 humidity == 0 (sensor fault) 17 negative wind / visibility / solar / rain / snow 0 dew_point > temperature (physically impossible) 0 solar_radiation > 0 between 22 h and 4 h 0 season label inconsistent with the month 0 snowfall > 0 with temperature > 5 °C 14 visibility at the 2000 (20 km) ceiling 2,245 (25.63%)

The 14 "snow above 5 °C" rows are plausible if snowfall records snow on the ground rather than new snow. They are kept. The 2,245 rows at visibility = 2000 are a sensor ceiling (censoring), not an error, so they are kept too.

Target leakage: functioning_day. In the 295 hours (3.37%) with functioning_day == "No", the target is always 0. These are exactly the 295 zero-target rows (0 zeros remain on functioning hours). Those hours fall on 13 days (12 of them closed for all 24 hours). They record times when the rental system was closed, not demand. The column is a deterministic rule, not a predictor (outputs/functioning_day_vs_target.csv).

Columns and rows to drop.

  • The 295 non-functioning rows are dropped. At prediction time, operators know whether the system is open, so the model only has to predict demand for open hours. After dropping, functioning_day is constant ("Yes"), so it is dropped too. 8,465 rows remain.
  • date is not a model input. It is used to group the split (1D) and to derive day_of_week. The year is not useful because the data cover a single year.
  • dew_point is redundant (3A). It is dropped inside the pipeline (4C).
  • There is no identifier column.

docs.text:
Target on the training set (n = 6,761, after 1D). The values on the full retained data are almost identical: mean 729.16, median 542.0, skewness 1.140.

Statistic Value mean / median 731.07 / 547.0 bikes/h std 640.69 min / Q1 / Q3 / P99 / max 2 / 214 / 1,087 / 2,522.6 / 3,418 skewness / excess kurtosis 1.125 / 0.752 skewness after sqrt 0.352 skewness after log1p -0.749

Figure 1. The raw target is right-skewed (skewness 1.125, mean 731 > median 547). Most hours have a few hundred rentals, and a long tail reaches 3,418. log1p overcorrects (skewness -0.749): it stretches the night hours with only 2-50 rentals into a left tail. Conclusion: train on sqrt(y) (skewness 0.352, the closest to 0), invert with a square when predicting, and report errors in bikes/h.

docs.title: 1D. Train/test split
docs.text:
• Method: StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42); the first fold is the test set (code/bike_preprocessing.py:split).

  • Strata = seasons: each season is in both sets in the same proportion. A purely temporal split (last 20% of the year) would put almost only autumn in the test set and no winter, so a model would be tested on a season it never saw.
  • Sizes: train 6,761 rows, test 1,704 rows (20.13%). The target is similar in both: mean 731.07 vs 721.55, median 547.0 vs 531.5.

docs.title: 3A. Numerical x numerical
docs.text:
Method: Spearman as the primary coefficient, Pearson for comparison. Rainfall and snowfall are 95% zeros with extreme tails, and the target is skewed. Pearson is dominated by a few extreme hours there, while Spearman measures monotonic association on ranks. The gap shows it: rainfall vs target is Pearson -0.118 but Spearman -0.275.

Figure 5. The most correlated pair is temperature - dew_point: Spearman 0.918 (Pearson 0.919). The next pairs are much weaker: - humidity - visibility: Spearman -0.491 - humidity - dew_point: 0.533 - humidity - solar_radiation: -0.432

Against the target, Spearman (Pearson in brackets):

Feature vs target temperature 0.617 (0.565) dew_point 0.426 (0.409) hour 0.423 (0.432) solar_radiation 0.413 (0.274) rainfall -0.275 (-0.118) snowfall -0.241 (-0.144) humidity -0.205 (-0.186) visibility 0.190 (0.209) wind_speed 0.141 (0.114)

Conclusion: temperature and dew_point are redundant. Dew point is a physical function of temperature and humidity: a linear fit on those two explains R² = 0.9916 of its variance. We drop dew_point and keep the two more interpretable inputs.

Figure 6. - Left: dew_point follows temperature along a tight band whose offset is set by humidity, which confirms the redundancy. - Middle: demand rises with temperature up to about 25 °C (binned median ~1,100 bikes/h) and then falls towards 35-40 °C. The relation is not monotonic. - Right: hour has two peaks (8 h and 18 h) and a trough at 4-5 h, which no linear term on hour can represent.

Conclusion: the main signals are non-linear and cyclical. That supports a neural network with a sin/cos encoding of hour over a linear model.

Precipitation acts like a switch rather than a gradient. In the 5.46% of training hours with rainfall > 0, the median demand is 86 bikes/h, against 587 in dry hours. In the 5.18% of hours with snowfall > 0 it is 149 against 588.

Target by category (training set; outputs/categorical_target_stats_train.csv):

Feature Level: mean / median (bikes/h) seasons Winter 223.0 / 197.5; Spring 759.2 / 610.5; Summer 1,026.1 / 886.5; Autumn 932.3 / 857.0 holiday No Holiday 744.0 / 568.0; Holiday 483.2 / 240.0 day_of_week Mon 744.8 / 573.0; Tue 721.1 / 533.0; Wed 775.0 / 608.5; Thu 682.9 / 455.5; Fri 802.3 / 640.0; Sat 765.1 / 589.0; Sun 639.8 / 422.5

Figure 7. - Season: the strongest categorical effect. The winter median (197.5) is about 4.5 times lower than summer (886.5), and winter's spread is also much narrower. - Holidays: the median is less than half that of normal days (240 vs 568). - Day of week: medians range only from 422.5 (Sun) to 640.0 (Fri), with large overlap.

Conclusion: seasons and holiday shift the target level. day_of_week alone shifts it little, but it changes the daily shape (Figure 8).

Figure 8. On working days (4,560 training hours), demand has a commuter shape: - a morning peak at 8 h (median 1,564); - the daily maximum at 18 h (median 1,946).

On weekends and holidays (2,201 hours), there is no morning peak (8 h median 412). Demand rises slowly to an evening plateau, with a maximum at 20 h (median 1,028). Conclusion: hour and day type interact. The model must be able to combine hour_sin/cos with day_of_week and holiday, which a network with hidden layers can learn and a purely additive model cannot.

Summer is the warmest (median 26.8 °C) and the most stable (IQR 6.6), while spring and autumn have similar medians (13.0 vs 12.6 °C) but the widest spread (IQR 10.3 and 11.7), because they are transition seasons. - Humidity: grows from winter (46%) to summer (65%). - Solar radiation: its spread triples from winter (IQR 0.42) to summer (1.36). - Visibility: spring has the lowest median visibility (13.25 km) and the largest spread, consistent with spring dust and haze.

Conclusion: season is partly a proxy for weather, but spring and autumn overlap in temperature, so season carries information beyond temperature (Figure 10).

Figure 10. At the same temperature, demand differs by season. Around 20 °C, the median is about 1,150 bikes/h in spring and autumn but about 600 in summer. In summer, demand peaks near 26.5 °C (about 1,040) and then falls to about 760 at 35.5 °C (heat and the humid monsoon). docs.title: 4. Preprocessing
docs.text:
Regression EDA, section 5 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

The destination is a neural network, which needs dense, finite inputs on comparable scales. Each choice below cites the finding that motivates it. Every statistic is fitted on the training set only (4C).

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text: Finding Strategy 0 NaN in all columns (1B) SimpleImputer in every branch (median for numerical features, most frequent for categorical). It changes nothing on this data but guards against NaN in future data. humidity == 0 in 17 hours, a physically impossible sensor fault (1B, Figure 2) Mask 0 to NaN, then impute with the training median of the valid readings (57%). Affected: 13 training rows and 4 test rows. functioning_day == "No" means target = 0 by rule (1B) Not a missing-value case: these 295 rows are removed before the split. In deployment, closed hours are predicted as 0 by rule.

docs.title: Outliers
docs.text:
Finding Strategy rainfall (skewness 15.32, max 35 mm) and snowfall (skewness 9.47, max 8.8 cm) have extreme tails (Figure 3), and demand is already near its floor once it rains or snows (3A: median 86 and 149 bikes/h) Cap at the training P99: rainfall at 4.0 mm, snowfall at 2.2 cm (QuantileClipper), then log1p. Training rows affected: 60 (rainfall), 56 (snowfall), 115 rows with at least one clipped value (1.70%). Test rows: 16, 41, 57 (3.35%). 0 rows removed. wind_speed, solar_radiation: moderate tails, physically valid (Figure 3) Not clipped; log1p compresses them. visibility at the 2000 ceiling (26.25% of training rows) Kept as is. The ceiling is censoring, not an outlier, and standardization keeps the ceiling as a single value.

The test clip rate is higher (3.35% vs 1.70%) because snowy days happened to fall more often into the test days (41 clipped snowfall hours from 1,704 test rows). The bounds stay those learned on train.

docs.title: Categorical encoding
docs.text: Finding Strategy seasons (4), holiday (2) and day_of_week (7) have low cardinality and no natural order usable by a network (2B) One-hot encoding, giving 13 columns. Categories that appear only in the test set OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"): an unseen level becomes an all-zero row instead of an error. None occurs in this test set (checked: 0 test-only levels for all three features). hour is cyclical: 23 h and 0 h are neighbours, and demand has two daily peaks (Figure 6, 8) Encode as hour_sin, hour_cos = sin/cos(2π·hour/24).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Finding (2A) Strategy temperature, visibility near-symmetric or bounded StandardScaler humidity near-symmetric, with the sensor zeros mask 0 → median impute → StandardScaler wind_speed (skewness 0.91), solar_radiation (1.48) right-skewed log1p → StandardScaler; skewness drops to 0.02 and 1.05 rainfall, snowfall zero-inflated, extreme tails P99 clip → log1p → StandardScaler; skewness drops from 15.32 to 5.59 and from 9.47 to 5.20 dew_point redundant with temperature (R² 0.9916, 3A) dropped target skewness 1.125 (1C) not in the X pipeline: train on sqrt(y) (skewness 0.352)

The remaining skewness of rainfall and snowfall is a property of the 95% zero mass, which no monotonic transform removes. After the transform, all non-zero values lie in a narrow range, which is what matters for gradient-based training.

Figure 11. The pipeline turns wind_speed into an almost symmetric feature (0.91 → 0.02). For solar_radiation, rainfall and snowfall it compresses the tail into a few standard deviations while keeping the zero spike (dry or night hours) as a separate value. Conclusion: no input to the network can reach the ~30 SD values seen in Figure 3.

docs.title: 4B. Dimensionality reduction
docs.text: The input is the 22 preprocessed training features (6,761 rows; the full training set, no subsample needed). Points are colored by log1p(rented_bike_count), with the color range clipped to P2-P98 for contrast.

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
Figure 12. PC1 explains 24.87%, PC2 16.73%, PC1 + PC2 = 41.60%. 7 components reach 80%, 11 reach 90%, and 15 reach 95%. The rank is 19, not 22: each one-hot group sums to 1, so 3 columns are linearly dependent.

  • PC1 (dry and sunny vs humid and overcast): humidity +0.54, solar_radiation -0.49, wind_speed -0.39, visibility -0.39, rainfall +0.25. Its correlation with log1p(target) is -0.449: humid, dark, still hours have low demand.
  • PC2 (warm season vs cold): temperature +0.69, snowfall -0.36, solar_radiation +0.31, rainfall +0.27, humidity +0.26, seasons_Winter -0.24, seasons_Summer +0.20. Its correlation with log1p(target) is +0.382.
  • The one-hot columns have near-zero loadings on PC1 and PC2. A 0/1 column has variance at most 0.25, against 1.0 for each standardized numerical feature, so PCA is dominated by the weather variables.

Conclusion: the linear structure is spread over many directions (2 PCs = 41.60%). In Figure 13 (left), demand is highest in the upper-left region (dry, sunny, warm). It is lowest at the upper right (high PC1: humid, rainy hours) and at the bottom (low PC2: winter), with gradual transitions and no sharp boundary.

docs.title: t-SNE
docs.text:
Figure 13. t-SNE with perplexity 30 (final KL divergence 1.173) and perplexity 50 (KL 1.218): - Both show four large horizontal bands (one per season, Figure 15) plus a smaller group at the right edge, which is mostly wet hours. - Inside each band, points form short curved strands: consecutive hours of the same day with similar weather. - Perplexity 50 gives a smoother, more global arrangement than 30, but the same groups. - The low-demand (light) points concentrate in the bottom band (winter) and in the right-edge group (wet hours).

Conclusion: unlike PCA, t-SNE separates discrete regimes. Distances between bands and band sizes have no direct meaning in t-SNE.

docs.title: UMAP
docs.text:
Figure 14. UMAP with n_neighbors = 15 and n_neighbors = 50 (min_dist 0.1): - n = 15 gives many small islands of similar hours. - n = 50 merges them into a few large groups, which is a more global view. - Two small groups have the lowest demand, with low values clustered inside them: one is made of rainy hours, the other of snowy hours. This matches 3A (median 86 and 149 bikes/h versus about 587 when dry).

Conclusion: UMAP isolates the precipitation regime as its own group. Distances between groups and their sizes are not interpretable.

docs.title: What t-SNE and UMAP reveal relative to PCA
docs.text:
Figure 15. - Coloring by season (top row) explains the large groups of t-SNE and UMAP: each is one season. PCA only shows a gradient from winter (bottom) to summer (top). The local methods separate the seasons because two rows in different seasons differ by √2 in the one-hot columns, which dominates small neighborhoods. Note that this separation partly reflects our encoding, not only the data. - Coloring by hour (bottom row) shows the strands inside each group are ordered by hour of day (the sin/cos encoding makes a continuous loop).

Conclusion: the data are organized by season → precipitation → hour-of-day trajectory. The target varies smoothly along those trajectories rather than forming separate clusters, as expected for a regression target. A network must learn those non-linear, interacting effects, and no 2-D projection makes the target linearly separable.

Coordinates of all embeddings: outputs/embeddings_train.csv.

docs.title: 5. Synthesis
docs.text: Regression EDA, section 6 of 7. Use Next at the bottom to keep reading, or open the full report on one page.

docs.title: 5A. Main findings
docs.text:
1. functioning_day leaks the target. All 295 closed hours have 0 rentals. They are removed, which leaves 8,465 rows (1B).
  2. The target is right-skewed (skewness 1.125). sqrt brings it to 0.352, better than log1p (-0.749) (Figure 1).
  3. Demand is driven by temperature (Spearman 0.617) and hour (0.423), both non-linearly. Temperature has a summer peak near 26 °C, and hour has two commuter peaks on working days (Figures 6, 8, 10).
  4. Precipitation switches demand off: median 86 bikes/h in rain and 149 in snow, against about 587 dry (3A, Figure 14).
  5. Interactions matter: hour x day type (Figure 8) and temperature x season (Figure 10).
  6. dew_point is redundant with temperature and humidity (Spearman 0.918; R² 0.9916) and is dropped (Figure 5).
  7. rainfall and snowfall are about 95% zeros with extreme tails. They are capped at the training P99 and log-transformed (Figures 2, 3, 11).
  8. Low-dimensional structure: season → precipitation → hour trajectories. PCA needs 7 components for 80% of the variance (Figures 12-15).

docs.title: 5B. Modelling risks and handling plan
docs.text: # Risk Evidence Plan 1 Temporal dependence between hours of a day 24 rows per day, smooth hour trajectories (Figure 15) Keep the split grouped by day. For validation and tuning, use GroupKFold on date inside the training set, never a row-level random K-fold. 2 Skewed target and heteroscedasticity: winter has a much narrower spread than summer Figure 1, Figure 7 Train on sqrt(y) (TransformedTargetRegressor). Report RMSE and MAE in bikes/h, plus MAE per season. 3 Few holidays (14 training days, 4.97%) 2B Check residuals on holiday hours separately. If they are poor, merge holiday into a "weekend/holiday" day type as in Figure 8. 4 Only one year of data: each calendar period is seen once 1A Do not add month or year trend features that the test set would extrapolate. Treat results as valid for this year's climate only. 5 Sensor artifacts: 17 zero-humidity hours and a visibility ceiling (26.25%) 1B, 2A Humidity zeros are imputed (4A). The visibility ceiling is kept; a model can learn it as one value. 6 Snowy days unevenly split between the sets (3.35% of test rows clipped vs 1.70% of train rows) 4A Report test error on snowy hours separately; do not re-split to "fix" it. 7 Deployment rule for closed hours 1B Predict 0 when functioning_day == "No" before calling the model.
